segments.caption: You flip a coin 10 times, and get 9 heads.
Is the coin rigged, or did you just get lucky? The p-value answers exactly that.
Here's the textbook definition, the one to use in interviews.
The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming that the null hypothesis is true.
In plain words: if nothing special were going on, how surprising would this data be?
The null hypothesis is the boring explanation: nothing special is going on.
The coin is fair. The friend is just guessing. The new button changes nothing.
Example one. Assume the coin is fair, and flip it 10 times, again and again.
9 or more heads happens only about 1% of the time.
So the p-value is 0.01. Very surprising for a fair coin, so we start to doubt it.
Example two: you got 6 heads instead.
A fair coin gets 6 or more heads 38% of the time. So p is 0.38.
Not surprising at all. No reason to doubt the coin.
So here's the rule.
Small p-value: surprising, so evidence against the null. Big p-value: not surprising, no evidence.
Most people draw the line at 0.05. Below it, the result is called statistically significant.
Example three: a taste test.
A friend claims they can tell two cola brands apart. Blindfolded, they get 10 out of 10 right.
The null hypothesis: they're just guessing. A guesser gets 10 out of 10 only about 1 time in 1,000.
So p is about 0.001. Far below 0.05, so it's significant.
Two mistakes interviewers love to test.
One: a p-value of 0.01 is not a 1% chance that the null is true. It's the chance of the data, if the null were true.
Two: a small p-value doesn't mean a big effect. It only says the effect is probably not zero.
So remember: the p-value tells how surprising the observed data would be, if nothing special were going on.
Small means surprising. Below 0.05 means significant.
Quick quiz!
A test gives a p-value of 0.30.
Is the result statistically significant?
No!
0.30 is above 0.05. Data like this could easily happen by luck.
